societies.name: Biting the Sun — Four-BEE’s quasi-robot provision
societies.work: Don't Bite the Sun / Drinking Sapphire Wine
societies.society: The domed city before the narrator’s desert exile

scope.period: Ordinary city life before the protagonist’s exile
exclusions: Desert exiles and their later handmade settlement
Other domes as additional copies of the same material model

societies.description:
Four-BEE’s quasi-robots supply daily needs, repair damage and replace human bodies. Residents can obtain goods without earning ordinary wages; payment involves expressing gratitude rather than performing productive labor. This gives city residents a strong material floor, although dependence on the city and the possibility of punitive exile make a perfectly unconditional guarantee too strong. Body replacement reinforces support but is not the sole reason this qualifies.

The same quasi-robots run the governing Committee, putting effective productive authority near the autonomous-machine end of control. Humans can request services without owning the system. The narrator repeatedly fails to find useful employment because machines already perform the tasks. A high nonworking estimate is therefore defensible as a broad editorial reading, with a wide interval allowing for meaningful personal art, study, care or exploration. Those activities still count as work when useful. The desert community is outside this point, and the other domes are not counted again merely because they have different names.

guarantees.basis: Robots actually provide daily goods, repair and bodily support without productive wage requirements; city membership and exile qualify the guarantee.

control.basis: Quasi-robots themselves govern through the Committee; requests and consumer choice do not establish human ownership.

nonworking.basis: The unsuccessful search for useful work and machine performance of routine tasks support a high editorial estimate, not a census; personal useful activity remains possible.

evidence.claim: Robots actually provide daily goods, repair and bodily support without productive wage requirements; city membership and exile qualify the guarantee.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

uncertainties: Reference-led provisional assessment; source limitations and editorial uncertainty remain explicit.

societies.name: Red Star — The Martian commonwealth
societies.society: Voluntary labor with automated production and free consumption

scope.period: The established Martian society visited by Leonid
scope.population: Organic Martians, explicitly used as a humanlike population comparison
exclusions: Machines as people in the labor denominator

societies.description:
Bogdanov’s Mars combines automated factories with freely available consumption. Production and labor needs are tracked through a statistical coordination system, while people choose unpaid work and can change occupations. Access to ordinary goods is therefore not a wage contract, and common living standards support a favorable guarantee estimate. This is an actual technological and distributive arrangement rather than a communist label alone. Resource pressures and the reference’s limited account of every necessity keep the estimate provisional.

The system is presented as a common productive order coordinated through information, so control is placed toward shared organic-person control, with a broad interval for the central institute’s practical authority. Statistical machinery is not assumed to be a sovereign AI. The population is Martian and is disclosed as an analogy to the human axes. Most inhabitants reportedly choose useful work despite being free not to do it. Voluntary factory supervision, medicine and science remain work; short days and unpaid participation cannot supply an all-age nonworking percentage, which remains unresolved.

guarantees.basis: Accessible editorial material explicitly links automatic production, free consumption and voluntary unpaid labor; common housing corroborates ordinary rather than solely elite access.

control.basis: Communal production and flexible voluntary participation suggest distributed control; the central statistical institute creates uncertainty, not evidence of autonomous AI sovereignty.

nonworking.basis: Most Martians reportedly work voluntarily; no all-age activity census permits a percentage. Martians are an explicit organic-person proxy.

evidence.claim: Accessible editorial material explicitly links automatic production, free consumption and voluntary unpaid labor; common housing corroborates ordinary rather than solely elite access.
evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

uncertainties: Reference-led provisional assessment; source limitations and editorial uncertainty remain explicit.

societies.name: Dunno — Sun City’s machine-supported access
societies.work: Dunno in Sun City / Dunno on the Moon
societies.society: Technological city with need-based goods and continuing design work

scope.continuity: Nosov’s book trilogy; Sun City economic reference corroborated in the next book’s opening
scope.period: The functioning city’s established provision, before Dunno’s temporary magical disruption
scope.population: Sun City’s organic miniature people, explicitly treated as a humanlike population proxy
exclusions: Dunno’s magic wand as productive infrastructure
Moon society as the same economy
Flower City’s later adoption as another point

societies.description:
Sun City’s technological economy is distinguished from the visitor’s magic wand. An opening passage in the next novel describes machines taking over clothing manufacture and goods being taken according to need, explicitly comparing the arrangement with Sun City. The city therefore has a concrete productive and allocation mechanism, rather than qualifying just because it is cheerful or futuristic. Guarantees are provisionally favorable, with uncertainty because the short passage does not establish a complete housing and healthcare charter.

The available references do not explain final ownership of the whole productive system clearly enough to score control. A shared-access interpretation is provisional and does not turn factories or civic coordination into sovereign AI. These inhabitants are miniature organic persons, disclosed as a comparison to humans. Designers still invent clothing styles and respond to preferences, while scientists and other residents pursue useful activities. Machines doing the sewing do not establish that everyone stops working. Nonworking stays unresolved, and neither Flower City’s later imitation nor magical disruptions create additional retained societies.

guarantees.basis: A bounded indexed primary opening links labor-saving clothing machines, need-based access and Sun City’s existing arrangement; the reference separates technology from the visitor’s magic.

control.basis: Final ownership and authority over city production are not established; communal-access regime remains provisional.

nonworking.basis: Design, research and other useful contributions continue; miniature organic inhabitants are an explicit proxy and no activity census is available.

review_notes: Reference-led batch: twelve ordered dispositions add three provisional records; uncertain material economies are immediately set aside.
The newly appended 48 leads are discovery entries, not retained objects. The first 64 expansion leads were already completely processed.
Four-BEE’s high nonworking value is explicitly an editorial estimate, allowing useful personal activity; neither resurrection nor receiving services is itself a work census.
Nosov’s city is supported by a bounded indexed opening passage, not a full novel read; magical manufacturing, false secondary summaries and lunar capitalist obstruction are not imported as proof.
Bogdanov’s voluntary work remains work, central statistics are not machine sovereignty, and organic Martians are an explicit population proxy.
Unrelated Andromeda engineering results, low-quality automatically generated summaries and unsupported precise rights were discarded.
